questions.topic: Responding to Different Forms of Accident
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish selected burns, scalds and bruise-producing injury mechanisms and identify simple hazards without diagnosing a real person.
questions.prompt: In two fictional descriptions, skin is injured by contact with a hot iron and by spilled hot water. Which description illustrates a dry-heat burn and which a scald? Explain the difference in cause.
questions.answer: The hot iron illustrates a dry-heat burn; spilled hot water illustrates a scald. A scald involves hot liquid or steam rather than the dry hot object in the first case.
questions.explanation: These supplied fictional mechanisms are classification examples, not a diagnosis or a reason to touch hot objects.

markingGuide.description: Matches the iron to a dry-heat burn.

questions.subject: Social and Citizenship Studies
questions.topic: Responding to Different Forms of Accident
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish selected burns, scalds and bruise-producing injury mechanisms and identify simple hazards without diagnosing a real person.
questions.prompt: A fictional classroom scene shows a cup of very hot water close to a desk edge and a puddle across the walking space. Identify a different accident risk linked to each hazard and describe one preventive change for each.
questions.answer: The cup could spill and scald someone; an adult can place it safely away from the edge and children. The puddle could lead to a slip or fall; keep people clear and have the spill dealt with promptly by a responsible adult.
questions.explanation: This is hazard reasoning in a fictional scene, not an instruction to handle hot water or clean a hazardous spill.

markingGuide.description: Links the hot liquid to a scald risk.
Gives a suitable adult-led change reducing that risk.
Links the puddle to slipping/falling and gives a suitable safe response.
